text:
The text presents two contrasting views on human nature through the lens of literature and philosophy. William Golding’s *Lord of the Flies* illustrates the theme of inherent evil, suggesting that humans are naturally savage and that civilization is a fragile veneer. In contrast, Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s philosophy posits that humans are naturally good and free, and that it is society which corrupts them.

The primary difference in presentation lies in their opposing conclusions about the source of human behavior. Golding attributes negative behavior to an internal, innate quality, while Rousseau attributes it to external societal structures. However, a similarity in their presentation is that both use the concept of a "natural state" to define humanity. Golding implies that the natural state, when stripped of social constraints, reveals savagery, whereas Rousseau argues that the natural state is one of freedom and goodness, which is lost only when social constraints ("chains") are imposed. Both perspectives rely on the tension between individual nature and social order to explain human conduct.
